decks.title: Employment — Part 1: Workers, Participation and the Changing Structure of Work
goals: Define a worker, the workforce and the labour force, and calculate the worker-population ratio
Interpret differences in participation between men and women and between rural and urban areas
Classify workers by status and describe how work is distributed across sectors
Explain jobless growth, casualisation and the informalisation of the workforce

slides.heading: Employment: Growth, Informalisation and Other Issues
slides.body_md: Part 1 — who counts as a **worker**, how many people work, **in what status**, and how the **structure of work** is changing.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: who is a worker, workforce and labour force, the worker-population ratio, status of workers, sectors and growth, and formal and informal work
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Every economy needs people to produce goods and services, and every family needs a source of income. In this chapter we ask who is counted as a worker in India, what kind of work people do, and why so much of it is irregular and unprotected. Part one builds the vocabulary; part two looks at unemployment and what the government does about it.

slides.heading: Who is a worker?
slides.body_md: A **worker** is anyone who takes part in an **economic activity** that adds to the production of goods and services — paid or unpaid.

rows: A farmer sowing wheat on her own land
A son helping unpaid in the family shop
A bank clerk absent this week with fever
Temporarily away from a regular job
A retired grandfather living on his pension
A pension is not payment for current work

visual.alt: Table of five imagined persons: a farmer, an unpaid helper in the family shop and a clerk on sick leave are workers; a full-time student and a pensioner doing no economic activity are not
visual.caption: The test is taking part in production, not being paid a wage.

slides.narration: Economists count a person as a worker if he or she takes part in producing goods or services. A wage is not required. A boy helping without pay in the family shop is a worker, and so is a clerk who is away for a few days with fever. A full-time student or a retired person who does no economic activity is not. The question is always: is this person contributing to production?

slides.heading: Workforce and labour force
slides.body_md: **Labour force** = workforce + the unemployed.

nodes.label: Not in the labour force: students, home-makers, the very old and young
Labour force: working or seeking work
Unemployed: seeking or available but without work

visual.alt: Tree: the population divides into those outside the labour force and the labour force; the labour force divides into the workforce, who are working, and the unemployed, who seek work but have none
visual.caption: Labour force = workforce + unemployed

slides.narration: Start with the whole population. Some people are outside the labour force: young children, full-time students, home-makers and the very old. Everyone else is in the labour force. Within it, those actually working form the workforce, and those seeking or available for work but without it are the unemployed. So the labour force is always larger than the workforce unless there is no unemployment at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the total
slides.body_md: What do we call the workforce together with those seeking work?
slides.narration: Remember the tree: working people plus job seekers. What name covers both groups together?

slides.heading: The worker-population ratio
slides.body_md: **Worker-population ratio** = workers ÷ population × 100. It shows what share of people takes part in production.

visual.alt: Table computing the worker-population ratio of an imagined district: 2,40,000 workers out of a population of 6,00,000 gives 40 per cent
visual.caption: A higher ratio means a larger share of people takes part in production.

slides.narration: To compare places of different sizes, we use the worker-population ratio. Divide the number of workers by the population and multiply by one hundred. In this imagined district, two lakh forty thousand workers out of six lakh people gives forty per cent. A higher ratio means a larger share of people is engaged in producing goods and services.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ratios for men and women
slides.body_md: An imagined village in Madhya Pradesh has 1,000 men and 1,000 women; 540 men and 260 women are workers.
bullets: Step 1 — Use each group's own population as the base.
Step 2 — Men: 540 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 54 per cent.
Step 3 — Women: 260 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 26 per cent.
Step 4 — All: 800 ÷ 2,000 × 100 = 40 per cent.

visual.alt: Table working out worker-population ratios in an imagined village: men 54, women 26, all 40 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined figures.

slides.narration: Let us practise. For men, five hundred and forty workers out of one thousand men gives fifty four per cent. For women, two hundred and sixty out of one thousand gives twenty six per cent. For the whole village, eight hundred out of two thousand gives forty per cent. A common mistake is to divide women workers by the total population; always use the group's own population.

slides.narration: Here are the same three ratios as bars. The women's bar is about half the men's. Does that mean women in this village work less? Not necessarily. Cooking, fetching water and caring for children take long hours, but they are not counted as economic activity. So part of the gap is a gap in what we measure, not only in what people do.

slides.heading: Who participates more?
slides.body_md: Three broad patterns in India.

rows: Much of women's household work is not counted
Poor farm families need every hand; townspeople study longer

visual.alt: Table of broad participation patterns: the ratio is higher for men than women, higher in rural than urban areas, and higher for rural than urban women, with reasons
visual.caption: Qualitative patterns only; check current survey reports for figures.

slides.narration: Three patterns stand out. Men have a higher ratio than women. Villages have a higher ratio than towns, because poor farm families need every member to work, while in towns more young people stay in school and college. And rural women are more often counted as workers than urban women, because they work on family farms and in family enterprises. These are broad patterns; the survey reports give exact figures.

slides.heading: Quick check: compute a ratio
slides.body_md: An imagined hill district has 80,000 people and 30,000 workers. What is its worker-population ratio?
slides.narration: Divide workers by population and multiply by one hundred. Watch out for options that use the wrong base.

slides.heading: Status of workers
slides.body_md: Workers are grouped by the **terms** on which they work.

rows: A farmer, a kirana shop owner, a potter
Hired regularly, paid a wage or salary, often with benefits
A bank clerk, a factory supervisor
Hired for a day or a few days, no security
A head-load worker, a farm labourer at harvest

visual.alt: Table of the three categories of workers by status: self-employed, regular salaried employees and casual wage labourers, with meanings and examples

slides.narration: Workers are also classified by status. The self-employed own and run their own enterprise: a farmer, a shopkeeper, a potter. Regular salaried employees are hired by someone else and paid regularly, often with benefits like paid leave. Casual wage labourers are hired for a day or a few days at a time, with no assurance of further work. Self-employment has long been the largest of the three in India.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: status shares in a block
slides.body_md: A survey of 500 workers in an imagined block of Rajasthan finds 260 self-employed, 155 casual and 85 regular salaried.
bullets: Step 2 — Self-employed: 260 ÷ 500 × 100 = 52 per cent.
Step 3 — Casual: 31 per cent; regular: 17 per cent. Check: the shares add to 100.
Step 4 — Interpret: most people work for themselves or by the day; secure jobs are few.

slides.narration: Add the three groups to get five hundred workers. Two hundred and sixty self-employed is fifty two per cent. One hundred and fifty five casual workers is thirty one per cent, and eighty five regular employees is seventeen per cent. The shares add up to one hundred, which is a quick check. The interpretation earns marks too: secure, regular jobs are the smallest group.

slides.heading: Where and for whom each status is common

rows: Own small farms; labour on others' farms
Offices, factories and services hire regularly
Fewer have the education or mobility for regular jobs

visual.alt: Table of status patterns: in villages self-employment and casual labour dominate, in towns regular salaried work is more common, and women are more often self-employed or casual

slides.narration: Status differs by place and by gender. In villages, most people farm their own small plots or labour on others' farms, so self-employment and casual work dominate. In towns, offices, factories and services hire regularly, so regular salaried jobs are more common. Women are more often self-employed or casual, partly because fewer have had the education and freedom to move that regular jobs often need.

slides.heading: Quick check: what status?
slides.body_md: A man hired by building contractors each morning at a labour chowk, with no written contract, is a…
slides.narration: Ask two questions. Does he own an enterprise? Is he hired on regular terms? If the answer to both is no, which status is left?

slides.heading: Work across the three sectors
slides.body_md: Farming still employs the **largest share** of workers, but its share is **falling**.

rows: Many workers, low output per worker
Construction a big source of new work

visual.alt: Table of the changing distribution of India's workers by sector: the primary share is falling but still largest, the secondary share rising slowly, and the services share rising fastest
visual.caption: Broad trends; no exact shares are given.

slides.narration: Since independence, the share of workers in farming and allied activities has fallen, but it is still the largest single share. Industry has gained a little, with construction an important source of new work. Services have gained the most. Yet output has shifted to services much faster than workers have, so many people remain in farming, where output per worker is low.

slides.body_md: **Jobless growth**: GDP rises much faster than employment.

slides.narration: Look at this imagined state. Over ten years, its output index climbs steeply, but the employment index rises only a little. This is called jobless growth. It happens when growth comes mainly from better machines and higher productivity rather than from hiring more people. Growth is still welcome, but it does not by itself solve the problem of finding work for a growing labour force.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: measuring the gap
slides.body_md: Output index: 100 → 150. Employment index: 100 → 110. How far did jobs lag output?
bullets: Step 1 — With a base of 100, growth in per cent is the new index minus 100.
Step 2 — Output grew 50 per cent; employment grew 10 per cent.
Step 3 — Gap: 50 − 10 = 40 percentage points.
Step 4 — Conclude: a sign of jobless growth.

visual.alt: Table: output index grows from 100 to 150 (50 per cent) while employment index grows from 100 to 110 (10 per cent)
visual.caption: With a base of 100, growth in per cent is simply the index minus 100.

slides.narration: Index numbers make growth easy to read. When the base is one hundred, an index of one hundred and fifty means fifty per cent growth, and one hundred and ten means ten per cent. So output grew fifty per cent while jobs grew only ten per cent, a gap of forty percentage points. Say percentage points, not per cent, when you subtract two percentages.

slides.heading: Casualisation
slides.body_md: A rising share of **casual** wage work in total employment.

visual.alt: Flow of casualisation: regular jobs grow slowly, firms prefer short-term hiring, new entrants take casual work, and the share of casual labour rises
visual.caption: Casualisation

slides.narration: Over several decades, the share of casual wage labour in India rose compared with regular jobs. Economists call this casualisation. Regular jobs grew slowly, many employers preferred short-term hiring, and new entrants to the labour force often found only casual work. Casual workers have the least security of all, so casualisation means more families depend on uncertain daily earnings.

slides.heading: Quick check: growth without jobs
slides.body_md: What does jobless growth describe?
slides.narration: Think back to the two lines on the chart. Which one ran ahead, and which one lagged behind?

slides.heading: Formal and informal sectors
slides.body_md: The **formal sector**: all public-sector units and private units hiring **10 or more** workers. Everyone else is **informal**.

rows: All public-sector units; private units hiring 10 or more workers
Farmers, own-account workers, small enterprises, casual labour
Provident fund, paid leave, pensions, labour laws

visual.alt: Table comparing the formal and informal sectors: who is in each, regularity of income, social protection and the ability to form trade unions

slides.narration: Workers are also divided by the sector they work in. The formal, or organised, sector includes every public-sector establishment and private establishments that hire ten or more workers. Its workers usually have regular incomes, social security and the right to form trade unions. The informal sector covers farmers, own-account workers, small enterprises and casual labourers, who mostly have none of these protections.

slides.heading: Informalisation
slides.body_md: A growing share of work is informal, **even inside large firms**.

nodes.label: Larger informal share of the workforce

visual.alt: Flow of informalisation: formal jobs grow slowly, firms hire on contract, most new work is informal, so the informal share of the workforce grows
visual.caption: Informalisation

slides.narration: Formal jobs have grown slowly. Many firms, including large ones, now hire through contractors, paying by the day or by the piece without benefits. So most new work created in recent decades has been informal. This trend is called informalisation. Remember that it is the terms of work, not the size of the employer, that decide whether a worker is formal or informal.

slides.heading: Can informal workers be protected?
columns:
**Why it matters**
- Most workers are informal
- Illness or old age can push families into poverty
- Low wages, no bargaining power

**What can help**
- Registration and social security
- Enforcing minimum wages
- Credit, skills and markets for small units

nodes.label: Credit, skills and markets for small units

visual.alt: Flow of measures to protect informal workers: registration, social security, enforcement of minimum wages, and credit, skills and markets for small units
visual.caption: Protecting informal workers

slides.narration: Since most Indian workers are informal, their welfare is central to the employment question. Measures that can help include registering informal workers so that health, accident and pension schemes can reach them, enforcing minimum wages and safe conditions, and giving small enterprises credit, skills and markets so that they can grow and pay better. Protection and productivity need to rise together.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Anyone taking part in economic activity, paid or unpaid
Output grows much faster than jobs
Rising shares of casual and informal work

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: worker, labour force, worker-population ratio, status of workers, jobless growth, and casualisation and informalisation

slides.narration: To sum up part one. A worker is anyone taking part in production, paid or not. The labour force is the workforce plus the unemployed. The worker-population ratio is higher for men and in villages. Self-employment is the largest status. Output has grown faster than jobs, and the shares of casual and informal work have risen.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Define a **worker** by taking part in production, not by earning a wage.
Use the **group's own population** as the base for its ratio; show the formula and the working.
When subtracting two percentages, write **percentage points**.
Formal or informal depends on **terms of work**: a contract worker in a big firm is informal.
Give a **reason** with every pattern (rural–urban, men–women); the reason earns the second mark.
3 marks = three distinct points; 5 marks = five points with an example or figure.
slides.narration: A few tips. Define a worker by participation in production. In numericals, write the formula, use the right base and show each step. Write percentage points when you subtract percentages. Judge formal or informal by the terms of work. And whenever you describe a pattern, add the reason; that is usually where the second mark lies.

decks.title: Employment — Part 2: Unemployment, Problems and Policies
goals: Explain who is unemployed and calculate unemployment from labour force data
Distinguish open, disguised and seasonal unemployment and explain why some are hard to measure
Explain the main employment problems in India
Evaluate how the government creates employment, including MGNREGA 2005

slides.heading: Employment — Part 2
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **unemployment**: its types, how it is measured, and what the **government** does about it.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: meaning of unemployment, its open, disguised and seasonal types, measuring it, problems, government policies and an appraisal
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we counted workers. Now we look at people who want work but cannot find enough of it. We will meet three kinds of unemployment that are common in India, see why some of them hide inside the workforce, and then examine the main ways in which the government tries to create jobs.

slides.heading: Who is unemployed?
slides.body_md: A person is **unemployed** if he or she is **not working** but is **seeking or available** for work.

rows: not working, but seeking or available for work?
not working and not seeking work?

visual.alt: Decision table: a person who is working is in the workforce; one who is not working but is seeking work is unemployed; one not working and not seeking work is outside the labour force

slides.narration: Being without work is not enough to be counted as unemployed. A full-time student or a retired person is not working, but is not looking for work either, so they are outside the labour force. A person is unemployed only if she has no work and is seeking or available for it. So the number of unemployed equals the labour force minus the workforce.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: counting the unemployed
slides.body_md: An imagined town has a labour force of 8,000 and a workforce of 7,600.
bullets: Step 1 — Unemployed = labour force − workforce.
Step 3 — As a share of the labour force: 400 ÷ 8,000 × 100 = 5 per cent.
Step 4 — Use the labour force, not the population, as the base.

visual.alt: Table computing unemployment in an imagined town: labour force 8,000 minus workforce 7,600 gives 400 unemployed, 5 per cent of the labour force

slides.narration: Eight thousand people are in the labour force and seven thousand six hundred are working, so four hundred are unemployed. As a share of the labour force that is five per cent. Notice the base: unemployment is compared with the labour force, because people outside it, such as students, are not looking for work.

slides.heading: Three kinds of unemployment

rows: Willing and able to work, but no work at all
More people on a job than needed; output would not fall if some left
Family farms and small family businesses

visual.alt: Table of three types of unemployment: open, disguised and seasonal, with what each looks like and where it is common

slides.narration: Three kinds are especially important in India. Open unemployment is the plainest: people willing and able to work find none, often educated young people in towns. Disguised unemployment hides on family farms where more people work than are needed. Seasonal unemployment comes and goes with the crop calendar, leaving farm workers idle for months between harvest and the next sowing.

slides.heading: Quick check: an electrician without work
slides.body_md: A trained electrician has searched for work for eight months without success. What type of unemployment is this?
slides.narration: He is willing, able and actively searching, yet has no work at all. Which type fits?

slides.heading: Worked example 5: spotting disguised unemployment
slides.body_md: Output of an imagined family plot as more members join the work.
bullets: Step 1 — Read where the output curve stops rising.
Step 2 — Output reaches its maximum with 4 workers.
Step 3 — With 7 working: 7 − 4 = 3 add nothing to output.
Step 4 — These 3 are disguisedly unemployed: busy, but not productive.

slides.body_md: True or false? A tea-garden worker idle in winter, when plucking stops, is disguisedly unemployed.
slides.narration: Ask yourself: is the idleness caused by too many hands on the job, or by the season?

slides.heading: Measuring employment
slides.body_md: Data come from the **Census**, the **labour force surveys of the National Statistical Office** and **employment exchanges**.

slides.narration: India measures employment through the Census once every ten years, through regular labour force surveys of the National Statistical Office, and through records of employment exchanges. Even so, disguised and seasonal unemployment are hard to capture, because the people affected are counted as workers for much of the year. Unpaid family work also blurs the line between working and idle.

slides.heading: The main problems

rows: Most new workers end up in informal work
Many hands, low output per worker
Graduates jobless while firms lack trained workers
A large source of talent left unused

visual.alt: Table of employment problems in India: slow growth of formal jobs, underemployment in farming, skills mismatch and low participation of women, with what each means for workers

slides.narration: Pulling the threads together, India faces four linked problems. Formal jobs have grown slowly, so most new work is informal. Farming still holds far more workers than it needs. Many educated young people lack the skills employers want. And women's participation remains low, leaving a great deal of talent unused. Good policy has to work on all four.

slides.heading: Quick check: jobs without takers
slides.body_md: A city has jobless graduates while firms cannot find welders and nurses. What does this point to?
slides.narration: The jobs exist and so do the job seekers. What is missing between them?

slides.heading: How the government creates jobs
slides.body_md: Three routes: **direct**, **indirect** and **programmes**.

nodes.label: Directly: hires in departments and public enterprises
Indirectly: its output and spending make other firms hire
Through programmes: wage employment, self-employment, skills

visual.alt: Tree of how the government creates employment: directly by hiring, indirectly through its output and spending, and through wage-employment, self-employment and skill programmes
visual.caption: Three routes

slides.narration: The government creates employment in three ways. Directly, by hiring teachers, nurses, clerks and engineers in its own departments and public enterprises. Indirectly, when its output and spending lead private firms to hire: a public power plant buys coal and transport, so mines and truck owners take on workers. And through programmes that provide wage employment, support self-employment and build skills.

slides.heading: Kinds of employment programmes

rows: Loans, subsidies and training to start an enterprise
A loan to open a repair shop

visual.alt: Table of employment programmes: wage employment on public works such as MGNREGA 2005, self-employment through loans and training, and skill development

slides.narration: Employment programmes come in three kinds. Wage-employment programmes offer paid work on public works such as ponds, roads and tree planting. Self-employment programmes give loans, subsidies and training so that people can start their own enterprises. Skill-development programmes train people for the jobs that firms need. Many schemes combine these approaches.

slides.heading: The rural employment guarantee
slides.body_md: **MGNREGA 2005**: a legal right to wage work for rural households.

nodes.label: Up to 100 days of unskilled work a year
Wages paid into accounts; allowance if no work in time

visual.alt: Flow of the rural employment guarantee: a rural household registers, adults ask for work, up to 100 days of unskilled work a year are provided, and wages are paid into accounts, with an allowance if work is not given in time
visual.caption: MGNREGA 2005 in brief

slides.narration: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act of two thousand and five turned rural wage work into a legal right. A rural household whose adults want unskilled manual work can demand up to one hundred days of it in a year. If work is not given in time, an unemployment allowance is due. Wages are paid into bank or post office accounts.

slides.heading: Weighing government policies
columns:
**Gains**
- Lean-season income for poor households
- Useful local assets
- Credit and skills for small enterprises

**Concerns**
- Delays in wages and fewer days than demanded in places
- Formal jobs still grow slowly
- Skills do not always match demand

rows: Assets such as ponds and roads
Fewer days given than demanded in places

visual.alt: Table weighing government employment policies: gains such as lean-season income, assets and credit and skills, against concerns such as delayed wages, fewer days than demanded and slow growth of formal jobs

slides.narration: How well have these policies worked? They have given income and some security to millions of poor households, built ponds, roads and other assets, and helped many start small enterprises. At the same time, delays in payments, uneven delivery and the slow growth of formal jobs limit their reach. A fair answer in the exam presents both sides and suggests improvements.

slides.heading: Quick check: a loan for a repair shop
slides.body_md: A young woman gets a subsidised loan and training and opens a mobile-repair shop. What kind of programme is this?
slides.narration: Is she being paid wages for public work, or helped to start her own enterprise?

slides.narration: To sum up part two. The unemployed are those seeking or available for work without it; their number is the labour force minus the workforce. Open, disguised and seasonal unemployment are the main types, and the last two are hard to measure. The government creates jobs directly, indirectly and through wage, self-employment and skill programmes such as MGNREGA.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Disguised = **output would not fall** if some workers left; seasonal = **no work in some months**.
Unemployed = labour force − workforce; compare with the **labour force**, not the population.
Direct vs indirect job creation: give one **example** of each.
MGNREGA: **up to 100 days**, **rural households**, unskilled manual work, allowance if no work in time.
Policy questions: state **gains and limits**, then a suggestion; keep the wording neutral.
slides.narration: Final tips for part two. Learn the test for disguised unemployment: output would not fall if some workers left. Use the labour force as the base for unemployment. Give a concrete example for direct and indirect job creation. State the features of the rural guarantee precisely. And in any policy question, weigh gains against limits before you suggest an improvement.

sections.heading: 1. Workers, workforce and labour force
sections.body_md:
A **worker** is a person engaged in any **economic activity**, that is, any activity that contributes to the production of goods and services. Payment is not the test: unpaid helpers in a family farm or shop are workers, and so are regular employees temporarily absent through illness. Full-time students, home-makers doing only household work, and pensioners doing no economic activity are not workers.

- **Workforce:** all persons actually working.
- **Unemployed:** persons not working but **seeking or available** for work.
- **Labour force = workforce + unemployed.** People who neither work nor seek work are outside it.

sections.heading: 2. Worker-population ratio and participation
sections.body_md:
**Worker-population ratio = (number of workers ÷ total population) × 100.** It indicates what proportion of the population is actively contributing to production; it is used to compare regions and groups.

**Broad patterns in India** (qualitative; the latest survey reports give figures):
- Higher for **men** than for **women**: much of the work women do at home is not counted as economic activity, and social norms limit women's paid work.
- Higher in **rural** than in **urban** areas: poor farm households need everyone's labour; in towns more young people study longer.
- Higher for **rural women** than for **urban women**: rural women work on family farms and enterprises.

sections.heading: 3. Status of workers and distribution across sectors
sections.body_md:
**By status:**
- **Self-employed:** own and operate an enterprise; the **largest** category in India.
- **Regular salaried employees:** hired on a regular basis and paid wages or salaries, often with benefits.
- **Casual wage labourers:** hired for short spells, with no assurance of continued work or social security.

**Rural vs urban:** self-employment and casual work dominate villages; regular salaried jobs are more common in towns. **Women** are more often self-employed or casual.

**By sector:** the share of the **primary sector** in employment has **declined** but is still the largest; the **tertiary** share has risen most and the **secondary** share somewhat. Output has moved towards services faster than workers, leaving many in low-productivity farming.

sections.heading: 4. Growth, casualisation and informalisation
sections.body_md:
**Jobless growth:** GDP has grown faster than employment, because much growth came from technology and productivity rather than from more hiring.

**Casualisation:** over several decades the share of **casual** wage labour rose relative to regular salaried work, so more workers depend on uncertain daily earnings.

**Formal sector:** all **public-sector** establishments and **private** establishments employing **10 or more** hired workers. **Informal sector:** all other enterprises and workers — farmers, agricultural labourers, own-account workers, small enterprises and casual labour.

**Informalisation:** a rising share of the workforce works informally, including **contract workers inside formal firms**. Causes: slow growth of formal jobs, cost-cutting through contract hiring, slower public-sector hiring.

**Protecting informal workers:** registration and social security (health, accident cover, pensions), enforcement of minimum wages and safety, and credit, skills and market access for small enterprises.

A rise in the share of casual wage labour in total employment.
A rise in the share of workers in the informal sector or on informal terms.

sections.heading: 5. Unemployment: meaning, types and measurement
sections.body_md:
A person is **unemployed** when he or she has no work but is seeking or available for it. **Unemployed = labour force − workforce.**

- **Open unemployment:** willing and able to work at the prevailing wage, but no work at all; common among educated youth in towns.
- **Disguised unemployment:** more persons engaged in an activity than required; withdrawing some would **not reduce output**. Common on small family farms.
- **Seasonal unemployment:** work available only in certain months, as in farming between harvest and sowing.

**Data sources:** the **Census of India**, the **labour force surveys of the National Statistical Office (NSO)**, and **employment exchanges**. Disguised and seasonal unemployment are hard to measure because the persons concerned appear to be working.

sections.heading: 6. Problems and government policies
sections.body_md:
**Problems:** slow growth of formal jobs; underemployment in farming; mismatch between the skills of job seekers and the needs of employers; low participation of women.

**How the government generates employment:**
1. **Directly** — hiring in its departments, services and public enterprises.
2. **Indirectly** — its output and investment raise demand for goods and services of private firms, which then hire.
3. **Programmes** — **wage employment** on public works; **self-employment** through loans, subsidies and training; **skill development** for jobs in demand.

**MGNREGA 2005:** a legal guarantee of up to **100 days** of unskilled manual wage work a year to every **rural household** that asks; an unemployment allowance if work is not given in time; wages paid into accounts; works such as water conservation and rural roads.

**Appraisal (balanced):** these measures have given income and security to many poor households and created assets, but implementation gaps (such as payment delays) and the slow growth of formal jobs limit their impact; better skills and labour-intensive growth are widely seen as the long-term answer.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying an unpaid family helper is not a worker: anyone taking part in production is a worker.
- Dividing women workers by the total population when asked for the women's ratio.
- Calling a contract worker in a large factory formal: the **terms** of work decide.
- Mixing up disguised unemployment (output would not fall) and seasonal unemployment (no work in some months).
- Writing that MGNREGA gives 100 days to each **person** or to **urban** youth: it is up to 100 days per **rural household**.
- Writing "per cent" for the difference of two percentages: it is **percentage points**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: one correct option or value.
- 2 marks: two points, or a definition with an example (about 30–50 words).
- 3 marks: three distinct points (about 50–80 words).
- 5 marks: five points with examples, data or a balanced judgement (about 80–120 words).

questions.stem_md: Meena, 19, spends the whole day helping her parents run their family dhaba on a highway in Haryana. She is not paid a separate wage. In employment statistics she is

options.text_md: not a worker, because she receives no wage of her own
a worker, because she takes part in an activity that produces a service and adds to GDP
unemployed, because she has no job outside the family
outside the labour force, because family members are never counted

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** a worker, because she takes part in an activity that produces a service and adds to GDP. Anyone who takes part in an economic activity counts as a worker, including unpaid helpers in a family enterprise. A wage is not the test; contributing to production is. She is neither unemployed nor outside the labour force.

questions.stem_md: Which of these persons in an imagined Pune household would **NOT** be counted as a worker?

options.text_md: Asha, who runs a beauty parlour from the front room
Vinod, a bank clerk on medical leave this week
Kamla, who helps her son sell vegetables from his cart every morning
Rohan, a full-time college student who does no paid or family work

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Rohan, a full-time college student who does no paid or family work. A full-time student who does no economic activity is not a worker. The parlour owner is self-employed; a regular employee temporarily absent due to illness is still a worker; an unpaid helper in a family enterprise is a worker.

questions.stem_md: The worker-population ratio of a country is a useful indicator because it shows

options.text_md: what proportion of the population is actively contributing to the production of goods and services
how many people are looking for work but cannot find it
the average wage earned by workers in a year
how many workers are employed by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** what proportion of the population is actively contributing to the production of goods and services. The ratio = workers ÷ population × 100, so it tells us what share of people take part in production. The number seeking work is unemployment; wages and government jobs are different measures.

questions.stem_md: An imagined hill district has a population of 80,000, of whom 30,000 are workers. Its worker-population ratio is

options.text_md: 30 per cent
62.5 per cent
37.5 per cent
2.67 per cent

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** 37.5 per cent. Ratio = 30,000 ÷ 80,000 × 100 = 37.5 per cent. 62.5 is the share of non-workers; the other two misuse the numbers.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes the **labour force** of an economy?

options.text_md: It includes only those who are actually working
It includes the whole population of working age, whether or not they want work
It includes those who are working and those who are not working but are seeking or available for work
It includes only workers in factories and offices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It includes those who are working and those who are not working but are seeking or available for work. Labour force = workforce (those working) + the unemployed (seeking or available for work). The workforce alone leaves out the unemployed; people of working age who do not want work, such as full-time students, are outside it.

questions.stem_md: In India, a larger share of rural women than urban women is counted as working. The best explanation is that

options.text_md: many poor rural households need every member's labour on farms and in family enterprises, while more urban women stay in education or home-based roles that are not counted
urban areas have no jobs open to women
rural women earn higher wages than urban women
the Census counts only rural women as workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** many poor rural households need every member's labour on farms and in family enterprises, while more urban women stay in education or home-based roles that are not counted. Rural families, often poor and working on their own land or as labourers, rely on women's work. In towns, more women from better-off households study or do unpaid household work, which is not counted as economic activity. Urban jobs for women do exist, rural wages are not higher, and the Census counts workers everywhere.

questions.stem_md: Shabana owns two sewing machines and stitches blouses to order in her house in Lucknow. Her status as a worker is

options.text_md: regular salaried employee
casual wage labourer
unemployed
self-employed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** self-employed. She owns and runs her own enterprise and earns from it, so she is self-employed. She is not hired by anyone, either regularly or by the day.

questions.stem_md: Ramesh waits at a labour chowk in Jaipur each morning and is hired for the day by building contractors, without any written contract. He is a

options.text_md: regular salaried employee
casual wage labourer
self-employed worker
formal-sector worker

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** casual wage labourer. Being hired by others for a day or a few days, with no regular job or social security, makes him a casual wage labourer. He does not own an enterprise, and with no contract or benefits he is not in the formal sector.

questions.stem_md: Which worker in an imagined city is a **regular salaried employee**?

options.text_md: A nurse employed by a hospital who gets a monthly salary and provident fund
A plumber who visits homes and charges each customer separately
A farm labourer hired for the harvest season
A woman who runs a tiffin service from her kitchen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A nurse employed by a hospital who gets a monthly salary and provident fund. A regular salaried employee is hired by someone else and paid regularly, often with benefits. The plumber and the tiffin service are self-employed; the harvest labourer is a casual worker.

questions.stem_md: Taking all of India's workers together, the largest category by **status** has long been

options.text_md: regular salaried employees
self-employed workers
casual wage labourers
government employees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** self-employed workers. Self-employment (farmers on their own land, shopkeepers, artisans, vendors) has long been the largest category, followed by casual wage labour; regular salaried jobs are the smallest share. Government employees are a part of regular salaried workers.

questions.stem_md: Regular salaried jobs form a much larger share of work in towns than in villages. Which reason best explains this?

options.text_md: Village people do not want regular jobs
Self-employment is banned in towns
Offices, factories and services that hire people on regular terms are concentrated in towns and cities
Casual work does not exist in towns

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Offices, factories and services that hire people on regular terms are concentrated in towns and cities. Enterprises that hire on regular terms — offices, larger factories, hospitals, banks, schools — are concentrated in urban areas and need educated, skilled workers. In villages most people farm their own land or work as casual labourers. The other options are false.

questions.stem_md: Under the commonly used classification, which establishments together make up the **formal sector**?

options.text_md: Only government departments and ministries
All enterprises that sell goods in a market
All farms, shops and workshops with at least one worker
All public-sector establishments and private establishments that employ 10 or more hired workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** All public-sector establishments and private establishments that employ 10 or more hired workers. The formal (organised) sector = all public-sector establishments + private-sector establishments hiring 10 or more workers. Everyone else (farmers, own-account workers, small enterprises) is in the informal sector.

questions.stem_md: Which of these workers is in the **informal** sector?

options.text_md: A clerk in a state government treasury office
An engineer in a public-sector power company
An accountant in a private firm employing 300 people on regular terms
A cobbler working on his own at a pavement in Patna

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A cobbler working on his own at a pavement in Patna. An own-account worker on the pavement has no employer, no protection and no regular income, so he is informal. Government and public-sector employees, and regular staff of a large private firm, are in the formal sector.

questions.stem_md: "Jobless growth" describes a situation in which

options.text_md: GDP falls while employment rises
both GDP and employment stop growing
GDP grows rapidly, but employment grows much more slowly or hardly at all
every new job is created by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** GDP grows rapidly, but employment grows much more slowly or hardly at all. In jobless growth, output rises (often because of better technology and productivity) without a matching rise in jobs. The other options describe different situations.

questions.stem_md: Economists speak of the **casualisation** of the workforce when

options.text_md: more workers get permanent jobs with social security
the share of casual wage labourers rises while the shares of self-employed and regular salaried workers fall
the workforce moves from services back to farming
the government raises the minimum wage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** the share of casual wage labourers rises while the shares of self-employed and regular salaried workers fall. Casualisation is the rising share of casual wage work in total employment — work that is irregular and insecure. More permanent jobs is the opposite; the sector shift and minimum wages are different ideas.

questions.stem_md: A large automobile company in an imagined industrial town hires half its workers through contractors, paid by the day, with no provident fund or paid leave. Economists would describe these workers as

options.text_md: informal workers inside a formal-sector firm, an example of informalisation
formal workers, because the company is large and registered
self-employed, because they are hired through contractors
public-sector workers, because the company pays taxes

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** informal workers inside a formal-sector firm, an example of informalisation. What makes work formal is its terms: regular contracts, social security and protection. Contract workers without these are informal even inside a large registered company; their growing share is informalisation. Contract labour is not self-employment, and paying taxes does not make a firm public.

questions.stem_md: Over the decades since 1950, how has the distribution of India's workforce across sectors changed?

options.text_md: The primary sector's share has risen steadily
The primary sector's share has fallen, though it still employs the largest share; the shares of the secondary and especially the service sector have risen
The service sector now employs more than three-quarters of all workers
There has been no change at all in the sector shares

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The primary sector's share has fallen, though it still employs the largest share; the shares of the secondary and especially the service sector have risen. The share of agriculture and allied work has declined but remains the largest single share; the secondary and tertiary sectors have gained, services more. The other options contradict this broad pattern.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The worker-population ratio for women in India is lower than that for men.

**Reason (R):** Much of the work that women do at home, such as cooking, cleaning and caring for the family, is not counted as economic activity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: unpaid household work is not counted as production for the market, so many women who work hard every day are not counted as workers, which lowers their measured ratio.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A rise in GDP does not always create a proportionate rise in employment.

**Reason (R):** Output can grow through better technology and higher productivity, so firms can produce more without hiring many more workers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: when growth comes from machines and productivity rather than more workers, jobs lag behind output (jobless growth).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Workers in the formal sector usually enjoy social security benefits.

**Reason (R):** The informal sector includes millions of farmers, agricultural labourers and owners of small enterprises.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R describes who is in the informal sector; it does not explain why formal workers get social security (labour laws and regular contracts do).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Casual wage labourers enjoy greater job security than regular salaried employees.

**Reason (R):** Casual wage labourers are hired for short periods and are not assured of regular work.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: casual workers have the least security. R is true and is exactly why they are insecure.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A boy who helps his father harvest wheat on the family farm during his school holidays is counted as a worker for the period he works.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** He takes part in production on the family farm, so he is a worker for that period, even without a wage.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A private bakery in Indore that employs 6 hired workers belongs to the formal sector under the commonly used classification.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** A private establishment is in the formal sector only if it hires 10 or more workers; with 6 hired workers the bakery is in the informal sector.

questions.stem_md: The workforce together with those who are seeking or available for work but cannot find it is called the ___.
questions.solution_md: Workforce + unemployed = labour force.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined worker in Kochi with their status in employment.

options.text_md: Thomas, who owns a small fishing boat and sells his own catch
Lissy, a teacher in a school on a monthly salary with a pension scheme
Biju, a loader hired by the day at the harbour
Anu, a graduate who has applied for many jobs and is still looking

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Owning and running one's own enterprise is self-employment; a regular wage with benefits is regular salaried work; daily hire is casual labour; seeking work without finding it is unemployment.

questions.stem_md: An imagined district in Odisha has a population of 5,00,000 and 1,90,000 workers. Calculate its worker-population ratio.
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Ratio = workers ÷ population × 100.
Step 2: 1,90,000 ÷ 5,00,000 × 100 = 38 per cent.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined village in Bihar there are 1,300 men and 1,200 women. 676 men and 324 women are workers. What is the worker-population ratio for **women**?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Use only the women: workers ÷ population × 100.
Step 2: 324 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 27 per cent (for men it is 52 per cent, and 40 per cent overall).

marking_scheme.step: Correct formula with the women's figures

questions.stem_md: A survey of an imagined block finds 208 self-employed workers, 120 casual wage labourers and 72 regular salaried employees. What percentage of the block's workers are self-employed?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Total workers = 208 + 120 + 72 = 400.
Step 2: Share = 208 ÷ 400 × 100 = 52 per cent.

questions.stem_md: Of 1,250 workers in an imagined small town, 125 work in the formal sector. What percentage work in the **informal** sector?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Formal share = 125 ÷ 1,250 × 100 = 10 per cent.
Step 2: Informal share = 100 − 10 = 90 per cent.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined district, casual wage labourers were 24 out of every 100 workers in one survey and 32 out of every 100 in a later survey. By how many percentage points did their share rise?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Shares are 24 per cent and 32 per cent.
Step 2: Rise = 32 − 24 = 8 percentage points, a sign of casualisation.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between the workforce and the labour force of an economy.
questions.solution_md: Define both; show that the labour force adds the unemployed to the workforce.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **workforce** is the number of people **actually working**, in any economic activity, paid or as family helpers.
2. The **labour force** is the workforce **plus the unemployed**, those who are not working but are **seeking or available** for work. So the labour force is the larger of the two.

marking_scheme.step: Labour force defined with the unemployed

questions.stem_md: Why is the worker-population ratio usually higher in rural areas than in urban areas of India? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: One reason about rural need to work; one about urban education or uncounted work.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Many rural households are **poor and own small farms**, so almost every member, including women and older children, **must work** to survive.
2. In towns, more young people **stay in education** longer and many women from better-off homes do unpaid housework, which is **not counted** as work.

marking_scheme.step: Rural households need every member to work
Urban schooling or uncounted household work

questions.stem_md: How do workers in the formal sector differ from those in the informal sector? Give two points of difference.
questions.solution_md: Two clear contrasts: regularity of work and income, and protection or benefits.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Formal** workers have **regular jobs and income**, while **informal** workers face **irregular** work and earnings.
2. Formal workers get **social security** such as provident fund, paid leave and pensions and can form **trade unions**; informal workers usually have **no such protection**.

questions.stem_md: Rafiq is a casual worker at a brick kiln; his cousin Salim is a regular salaried employee of a cooperative bank. Compare their positions on two grounds.
questions.solution_md: Compare on job security and on benefits, naming both workers.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Security:** Salim is employed **all year** with a fixed salary; Rafiq is hired **only when work is available** and may be idle for weeks.
2. **Benefits:** Salim gets **provident fund, paid leave** and medical cover; Rafiq gets **only his daily wage**, with no social security.

questions.stem_md: Explain three reasons why self-employment is the largest source of work in rural India.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct reasons: land cultivation, family enterprises because of scarce jobs, and skills limiting salaried work.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Most rural families **own or rent small plots** and cultivate them themselves, so they count as self-employed farmers.
2. Many run **family enterprises** such as dairies, small shops, handicrafts or repair work, because **regular jobs** in villages are **scarce**.
3. Low levels of **education and skills** limit access to salaried jobs, so people create their **own work** with family labour and little capital.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why an increasing share of workers has ended up in the informal sector in recent decades.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct causes: slow formal job growth, contract hiring by firms, and slower public hiring with migration into small enterprises.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Formal jobs grew slowly**: many firms raised output with **machines** rather than workers, so most new workers found only informal work.
2. Many firms prefer **contract and casual hiring**, which **cuts costs** and avoids long-term obligations.
3. Fewer new **public-sector jobs** were created, and young people moving off farms joined **small enterprises and self-employment** in towns.

questions.stem_md: Suggest three measures to improve the condition of workers in the informal sector, and say briefly why each would help.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct, workable measures, each with a reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Register** informal workers and extend **social security** (health insurance, accident cover, old-age pensions), so that illness or old age does not push families into poverty.
2. Enforce **minimum wages** and safe working conditions, so that employers cannot pay far below a fair rate.
3. Provide **cheap credit, skills and market links** to small enterprises, so that they grow, become more **productive** and pay better.

questions.stem_md: Explain the three categories of workers by status of employment, and describe how their shares differ between rural and urban areas and between men and women in India.
questions.solution_md: Define the three categories, then compare rural with urban and men with women, with a reason for each pattern.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Self-employed:** own and run an enterprise (farmers, shopkeepers, artisans); the **largest category** overall.
2. **Regular salaried employees:** hired on a regular basis with fixed pay and often benefits.
3. **Casual wage labourers:** hired for short periods without security.
4. **Rural vs urban:** in villages, **self-employment and casual labour** dominate because most people farm or labour on farms; in towns, **regular salaried jobs** are far more common because offices and factories are located there.
5. **Men vs women:** women are **more often self-employed or casual** and less often in regular jobs, which needs more education and mobility.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the informalisation of the workforce? Explain its causes and evaluate its effects on workers.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, causes, two effects and a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning:** a rising share of workers in the **informal sector**, or on informal terms (contract, casual) even inside formal firms.
2. **Causes:** formal jobs grew slowly as firms adopted **labour-saving technology**; firms use **contract labour** to cut costs; public-sector hiring slowed.
3. **Effects on income:** informal workers get **irregular, often low** earnings.
4. **Effects on security:** **no provident fund, paid leave or pension**, and little bargaining power through unions.
5. **Evaluation:** informal work still **absorbs millions** who would otherwise have no work, and gives some flexibility; the task is to **extend protection** and skills to it, not merely to replace it.

questions.stem_md: Describe the main changes in the structure of employment in India since independence: across sectors, by status, and in relation to the growth of GDP.
questions.solution_md: Cover sector shares, status (casualisation), informal growth, jobless growth and what it means.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Across sectors:** the share of the **primary sector** in employment has **fallen**, though it remains the largest; the **services** share has risen most, with some rise in industry.
2. **By status:** **self-employment** remains the largest category, but over several decades the share of **casual wage labour** rose relative to regular jobs (**casualisation**).
3. **Formal vs informal:** most new work has been **informal**, so the formal sector's share stays small.
4. **Jobs and GDP:** GDP has grown **faster than employment**, a pattern called **jobless growth**.
5. **Meaning:** output has shifted to services and industry faster than workers have, so many remain in **low-productivity** farm and informal work.

questions.stem_md: A trained electrician in Kanpur has been searching for work for eight months and is willing to work at the going wage, but finds none. This is an example of

options.text_md: disguised unemployment
seasonal unemployment
voluntary idleness
open unemployment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** open unemployment. He is willing and able to work at the prevailing wage and is actively looking, but has no work at all: open unemployment. Disguised unemployment hides inside a farm or family business; seasonal unemployment follows a crop calendar; he is not idle by choice.

questions.stem_md: Six members of a family work on their two-acre plot in an imagined Bihar village. If two of them took jobs in a nearby town, the farm's output would not change. The two members are

options.text_md: disguisedly unemployed
openly unemployed
seasonally unemployed
regular salaried workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** disguisedly unemployed. They appear to be working, but their contribution to output is nil, because output would not fall without them: disguised unemployment. They are not openly jobless, their idleness is not tied to a season, and they are not salaried.

questions.stem_md: Labourers in an imagined rain-fed district of Telangana find farm work during sowing and harvest but sit idle for several months in between. This is

options.text_md: disguised unemployment
educated unemployment
seasonal unemployment
jobless growth

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** seasonal unemployment. Unemployment that follows the farm calendar, with no work in certain months, is seasonal. Disguised unemployment involves surplus workers while work is going on; educated unemployment and jobless growth are different ideas.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a major source of data on employment and unemployment in India?

options.text_md: Annual reports of private companies
The Union Budget speech
Periodic labour force surveys conducted by the National Statistical Office
Election results

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Periodic labour force surveys conducted by the National Statistical Office. Employment data come mainly from the Census of India, the labour force surveys of the National Statistical Office and the records of employment exchanges. Company reports, budget speeches and election results are not employment surveys.

questions.stem_md: When a state government recruits teachers for its schools, it creates employment

options.text_md: directly
indirectly
only in the private sector
without any effect on the labour market

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** directly. Hiring people into government departments and services is direct job creation by the government. Indirect creation happens when government output or spending leads other firms to hire.

questions.stem_md: A public-sector fertiliser plant in an imagined district expands output. Nearby, transporters, packaging units and repair workshops hire more workers. The jobs in these firms are an example of

options.text_md: direct job creation by the government
disguised unemployment
casualisation of the workforce
indirect job creation by the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** indirect job creation by the government. The plant's own new posts are direct jobs; jobs that arise in other firms because the plant buys their goods and services are created indirectly. Neither disguised unemployment nor casualisation is described.

questions.stem_md: A government programme gives rural households paid manual work on public works such as ponds and roads. It is best described as a

options.text_md: self-employment programme
wage-employment programme
disinvestment programme
programme of import substitution

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** wage-employment programme. Providing paid work on public works is wage employment. Self-employment programmes help people start their own enterprises with loans and training; the other two are unrelated policies.

questions.stem_md: Rekha, an unemployed young woman in an imagined Assam town, gets a subsidised bank loan and training under a government scheme and opens a mobile-repair shop. The scheme is an example of

options.text_md: a self-employment programme
a wage-employment programme
direct recruitment into government service
a programme for formal-sector workers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** a self-employment programme. Helping a person set up her own enterprise with credit and skills is a self-employment programme. She is not hired for wages or into government service, and her small shop is in the informal sector.

questions.stem_md: Under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, 2005, the legal guarantee is for

options.text_md: a permanent government job for one member of every family
up to 100 days of unskilled manual wage work in a year for every rural household whose adults want it
100 days of paid training for urban graduates
free land for every landless labourer

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** up to 100 days of unskilled manual wage work in a year for every rural household whose adults want it. The Act guarantees up to 100 days of wage employment a year to each rural household whose adult members volunteer for unskilled manual work. It does not give permanent jobs, training for urban graduates or land.

questions.stem_md: An imagined city has thousands of jobless graduates, while local firms say they cannot find trained welders, electricians and nurses. This mainly points to

options.text_md: disguised unemployment in agriculture
a rise in the worker-population ratio
a mismatch between the skills people have and the skills employers need
seasonal unemployment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a mismatch between the skills people have and the skills employers need. Jobs exist but go unfilled while educated people stay unemployed, so the problem is a skills mismatch, calling for vocational and technical training. The other options do not fit an urban, educated, year-round situation.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Government spending on roads can create jobs in many private firms.

**Reason (R):** The government is a large employer in India through its departments and public enterprises.

Choose the correct option.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A tea-garden worker in Assam who is idle in the winter months, when picking stops, suffers from disguised unemployment.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Idleness linked to the crop calendar (no plucking in winter) is seasonal unemployment, not disguised unemployment, which is about surplus workers while work continues.

questions.stem_md: When more people are engaged in a job than are actually needed, so that removing some would not reduce output, the situation is called ___ unemployment.
questions.solution_md: This is disguised (hidden) unemployment.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the steps by which a new public-sector steel plant in an imagined district creates jobs indirectly, in the correct order.

options.text_md: These supplier firms hire more workers
The government invests in the new steel plant
Mines, transporters and suppliers receive more orders
The plant starts production and buys iron ore, coal and transport services

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Investment comes first, then the plant's purchases from other firms, then more orders for those firms, and finally new hiring in them.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined situation in rural and urban India with the type of unemployment it shows.

options.text_md: Five brothers work a one-acre plot that two could manage
Sugarcane cutters have no work after the crushing season ends
A diploma holder in Bhopal looks for work every day but finds none

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(q), (c)–(p). Surplus workers on a small plot are disguisedly unemployed; idleness after a crop season is seasonal; a job seeker with no work at all is openly unemployed.

questions.stem_md: An imagined town has a labour force of 5,200 and a workforce of 4,940. How many people are unemployed? (Also note what share of the labour force they form.)
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Unemployed = labour force − workforce = 5,200 − 4,940 = 260.
Step 2: Share = 260 ÷ 5,200 × 100 = 5 per cent of the labour force.

questions.stem_md: 7 members of an imagined family work on their farm. The same output could be produced by 4 of them. How many members are disguisedly unemployed?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Disguised unemployment = workers engaged − workers needed.
Step 2: 7 − 4 = 3 persons.

questions.stem_md: By December, an imagined household in Chhattisgarh has received 64 days of work under the rural employment guarantee in the current year. Up to how many more days of work can it still demand this year under the 100-day guarantee?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Guarantee = 100 days a year per household.
Step 2: Days left = 100 − 64 = 36 days.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined state, an index of output rose from 100 to 160 over ten years, while an index of employment rose from 100 to 115. By how many percentage points did output growth exceed employment growth?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Output growth = (160 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 60 per cent; employment growth = (115 − 100) ÷ 100 × 100 = 15 per cent.
Step 2: Gap = 60 − 15 = 45 percentage points, a sign of jobless growth.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between disguised unemployment and seasonal unemployment, with an example of each from rural India.
questions.solution_md: One definition and example for each type.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Disguised:** more people work on a task than needed, so removing some would **not reduce output**, e.g. six family members on a plot that **three could manage**.
2. **Seasonal:** people have work only in **certain months**, e.g. farm labourers idle between **harvest and the next sowing**.

questions.stem_md: With one example each, explain how the government creates employment directly and indirectly.
questions.solution_md: One direct and one indirect route, each with a clear example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Directly:** by hiring people in its own departments and enterprises, e.g. recruiting **nurses for government hospitals**.
2. **Indirectly:** its output or spending leads **other firms to hire**, e.g. a public **power plant** that buys coal and transport, so mines and truck operators take on more workers.

questions.stem_md: Name the main sources of data on employment in India and state one use of such data.
questions.solution_md: Name the sources; give one purpose.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Sources:** the **Census of India**, the **labour force surveys of the National Statistical Office**, and the records of **employment exchanges**.
2. **Use:** they show the size and **pattern of the workforce** and unemployment, which helps the government **design and target** employment policies.

questions.stem_md: Explain two features of the rural employment guarantee under MGNREGA 2005 that make it different from an ordinary government scheme.
questions.solution_md: Two features that turn work into a legal entitlement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Work is a **legal guarantee**: a rural household can **demand** up to **100 days** of unskilled manual work a year.
2. If work is not provided within the time fixed, the household is entitled to an **unemployment allowance**, so the state is **accountable** for delivering it.

marking_scheme.step: Legal guarantee of up to 100 days on demand

questions.stem_md: Suggest three ways in which India could make its economic growth create more jobs.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct, workable measures linked to more jobs per unit of growth.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Promote **labour-intensive industries** such as textiles, food processing, leather and tourism, which employ many people per unit of output.
2. Support **small and micro enterprises** with credit, simpler rules and market access, since they employ most non-farm workers.
3. Invest in **skills and vocational training**, so that workers can fill the jobs that growing firms create.

questions.stem_md: Describe three kinds of programmes through which the government has tried to generate employment in India.
questions.solution_md: Three kinds of programme, each described.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Direct employment** in government departments and **public enterprises**.
2. **Wage-employment programmes** that offer paid work on **public works**, such as the rural employment guarantee under **MGNREGA 2005**.
3. **Self-employment programmes** that give **loans, subsidies and training** to help people start small enterprises; skill-training schemes support both.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the rural employment guarantee as a policy: give two benefits and one limitation.
questions.solution_md: Two benefits and one limitation, each explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Benefit:** it gives rural households **income in the lean season**, which reduces hunger and **distress migration**.
2. **Benefit:** works such as **ponds, check dams and rural roads** build assets that can raise farm output.
3. **Limitation:** **delayed wage payments** and fewer days than demanded in some areas reduce its usefulness, so better **implementation** is needed.

questions.stem_md: Explain the main types of unemployment found in India. Why are some of them hard to measure?
questions.solution_md: Three types with Indian contexts, then two reasons why measurement is difficult.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Open unemployment:** people willing and able to work at the going wage find **no work at all**; common among educated youth in towns.
2. **Disguised unemployment:** more workers than needed on **family farms** or businesses; output would not fall if some left.
3. **Seasonal unemployment:** farm workers have work only in **sowing and harvest** months.
4. **Hard to measure:** the disguised and seasonally unemployed **appear to be working** for much of the year, so surveys count them as workers.
5. Also, much rural work is **unpaid family work**, so the line between working and idle is blurred.

marking_scheme.step: Why disguised and seasonal are hidden

questions.stem_md: Critically examine the role of the government in generating employment in India.
questions.solution_md: Four channels, then a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Direct jobs:** the government hires in its departments, schools, hospitals and **public enterprises**.
2. **Indirect jobs:** public investment in **power, roads and industry** raises output and hiring in private firms.
3. **Wage employment:** schemes such as **MGNREGA 2005** give rural households paid work on public works in the lean season.
4. **Self-employment and skills:** subsidised **loans and training** help people start enterprises.
5. **Assessment:** these schemes have given **income and some security** to millions, but problems of **implementation**, slow growth of formal jobs and skill gaps limit their reach; better targeting and **skills** remain the key.

questions.stem_md: Agriculture still employs the largest share of India's workers, yet much of this work is underemployment. Suggest and explain five measures to create productive jobs for rural workers.
questions.solution_md: Five distinct measures, each tied to how it creates productive work.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Irrigation and water works** (check dams, canals) allow a **second crop**, giving work for more months of the year.
2. **Rural roads, storage and markets** create jobs in **transport, trade and warehousing**.
3. **Agro-processing units** (dairy, rice mills, fruit products) near villages add value and hire local workers.
4. **Cheap credit and SHGs** help households start **non-farm enterprises** such as poultry, tailoring and repair work.
5. **Skill training** prepares rural youth for jobs in construction, services and manufacturing in nearby towns.

questions.stem_md: Read the report from an imagined gram panchayat on wage-employment works and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined panchayat, people and an imagined wage of ₹250 a day, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:

Step 2: 3,200 × 250 = ₹8,00,000.

**(b)** Step 1: Average = person-days ÷ households.

**(c) (i)** Two effects beyond wages, both from the report.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two reasons or remedies linked to the report.

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** **40 days**

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Give two pieces of evidence from the report that the works helped the village beyond paying wages.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Fewer young men migrated** to brick kilns in summer, so families stayed together with local income. (2) The **deeper tank holds water until March**, which can support a **second crop** and more farm work.

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Households got about 40 days on average against a guarantee of 100. Suggest two reasons for the gap or two ways to improve delivery.
alternatives.solution_md: Two reasons or remedies linked to the report.
